title: An exploration of the roles of cognitive reactivity and ego depletion in the relationship between entrapment and suicidal ideation
abstract: Abstract Objectives Entrapment is theorized as a key driver of suicidal ideation, yet the cognitive processes leading to entrapment, particularly the activating role of negative affect, and those through which entrapment translates into suicidal ideation are not well understood. Grounded in the Integrated Motivational‐Volitional Model, this study used mediation analyses to examine cognitive reactivity in relation to suicidal ideation via entrapment, and ego depletion as a mediator of the entrapment–suicidal ideation link. Design A cross‐sectional online survey was used to collect self‐report data from participants recruited through opportunity sampling. Methods The sample consisted of 312 adults living in the United Kingdom. Data analyses were conducted on a subsample of participants who reported a lifetime history of suicidal ideation and/or suicide attempts ( N = 269; M age = 28.50, SD = 10.06; 82.9% White; 66.5% female). Results The relationship between cognitive reactivity and suicidal ideation was accounted for by entrapment; this indirect association was not moderated by trait mindfulness. Additionally, the entrapment–suicidal ideation relationship was partially accounted for by self‐regulatory fatigue, but not by depletion sensitivity; this indirect effect remained significant after controlling for depression, but not anxiety diagnosis. Conclusions The findings highlight cognitive reactivity as a cognitive vulnerability to suicidal ideation and underscore the value of understanding suicide risk through the lens of self‐regulation. The cross‐sectional design limits causal inference, and the observed associations should be interpreted as correlational in nature.
